def merge_intervals(intervals: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
    """Merge overlapping or touching closed integer intervals.

    Given a list of closed intervals [start, end] with start <= end, return a
    new list of intervals sorted by start, in which any intervals that overlap
    or touch (e.g. [1, 3] and [3, 5]) are merged into a single interval.

    The input list is not mutated, and the returned intervals are new list
    objects, so modifying the result will not affect the input.

    Args:
        intervals: A list of [start, end] pairs (lists) with start <= end.

    Returns:
        A new list of merged intervals sorted by start. Returns [] for an
        empty input list.
    """
    # Handle the empty input up front so the main loop can assume at least
    # one interval exists.
    if not intervals:
        return []

    # Sort a shallow copy of the input by start value. Sorting a copy (rather
    # than the input itself) guarantees the caller's list is never mutated.
    # Sorting is O(n log n) and is what makes the linear merge scan possible:
    # once sorted, any interval that overlaps a previous one must overlap the
    # most recently merged interval.
    sorted_intervals = sorted(intervals, key=lambda interval: interval[0])

    # Start the result with a copy of the first interval so we never place a
    # reference to an input interval into the output (avoids aliasing).
    merged: list[list[int]] = [list(sorted_intervals[0])]

    # Single linear scan over the sorted intervals: O(n) after the sort.
    for start, end in sorted_intervals[1:]:
        last = merged[-1]

        # Because the intervals are sorted by start, the current interval can
        # only overlap or touch the last merged interval. "Touching" means
        # start == last[1] (closed intervals sharing an endpoint), so the
        # condition uses <= rather than <.
        if start <= last[1]:
            # Overlap or touch: extend the last merged interval if the
            # current interval reaches further right. We only ever grow the
            # end, never shrink it, since starts are non-decreasing.
            if end > last[1]:
                last[1] = end
        else:
            # No overlap: the current interval starts a new, disjoint merged
            # interval. Copy it so the output doesn't alias the input.
            merged.append([start, end])

    return merged
